title: Path of Lucas by Susanne Bellefeuille: Author, Context and an Important Correction
summary: The novel, its family-saga background and why the lesson note's story of a paralysed hockey star does not match published descriptions of the book.

p: Path of Lucas is a novel by the Canadian author Susanne Bellefeuille. Published guides describe it as a family drama based partly on the author's own family: the character Lucas is modelled on her father. It is one of the non-African prose set texts for the West African senior secondary Literature in English syllabus.

Your lesson note describes Lucas as a young star hockey player who is paralysed in a championship game, with a girlfriend Jessica and a physical therapist Sarah who becomes his love. The lesson note itself says that it is giving 'likely events'. Published summaries of the novel describe a quite different story: Lucas Clarkson is a farmer's son in Ontario in the 1950s; the story is told as a long life story that he tells to his daughter Lucy, who lies in a coma after a car crash; the main love is his wife, Isabelle Bourgeois.

So the names Jessica and Sarah, the hockey injury, the wheelchair rugby climax and the 'first-person' point of view in your lesson note should not be used as facts about the book. Take the story from the novel itself and use the next unit only as an outline to check.

sections.h: What you can still use from the lesson note
p: The method: analyse the plot stages, the characters, the setting, the themes and the narrative technique. The theme of endurance in the face of loss also fits the real story, though the losses are different.
Read the novel. Make a table of the main events in order, with the year or the character's age. In an exam, write about events and names you can find in the book.

title: Path of Lucas: The Story as Published Guides Describe It
summary: The main events in order: the hospital frame, 1956, marriage, the return to the farm, the family's losses and the ending.

p: This outline comes from published study guides; check it against your copy. Read the novel to confirm the order, the dates and the names.

Lucas's daughter Lucy is badly hurt in a car crash on her way to visit him and falls into a deep coma. Lucas keeps vigil at her bedside in the hospital and promises to tell her the story of his life to anchor her to the living world.
1. In 1956, at seventeen, Lucas meets the shy Isabelle Bourgeois on a country road. She tells him that she and her sister France were abused by their parents.
2. Lucas proposes on her eighteenth birthday. When she finds she is pregnant they marry in November 1958. Their children are born over the years: Richard, Johnny, Steve, Lucy and Thomas.
3. Lucas leaves the farm to train as a mechanic in Uxbridge, but his father, facing bankruptcy, asks him to come home to save the farm. Lucas gives up the job and returns to Alexandria, Ontario.

4. The 1970s bring many losses: the deaths of his friend Steve and his nephew Darcy, and the sudden death of Isabelle's sister France. Isabelle falls into a severe depression and for a time does not recognise Lucas.
5. Lucas gives up his job to take her out of the psychiatric ward. After a long struggle she recovers her memory and is reunited with her children.

6. Their eldest son Richard is diagnosed with throat cancer, goes into remission, then relapses and dies at twenty-two. Lucas sees a monarch butterfly and takes it as a sign that Richard is free of pain.
7. Lucas's parents die. Isabelle takes charge of her health and the couple enjoy years of travel.
8. In June 1993, Isabelle dies suddenly of a cardiac arrest at fifty-three.

In the present, Lucas finishes his story and Lucy begins to wake. After she recognises her family, Lucas collapses in the hospital corridor and dies of a heart attack, seeing a young Isabelle reaching out to him. A week later Lucy, who has recovered, gives the eulogy at his funeral.

Make your own Freytag chart from the book. The frame story gives a simple structure: exposition (the crash and the vigil), rising action (the life story and its losses), climax (Lucy begins to wake and Lucas's death), resolution (the funeral and Lucy's eulogy). Decide with your teacher where you place the climax.

title: Path of Lucas: Characters and Setting
summary: The main characters, the places of the story and how setting and time structure the novel.

p: Study the table; check the details in the book.

head: Character
Role
rows: Protagonist and narrator of his life story; a farmer's son who gives up his dreams out of duty and love
His daughter, a mother and professional, in a coma after a crash; she hears his story and wakes
His wife; shy, abused as a child, later suffers severe depression and recovers
Isabelle's older sister; dies suddenly at thirty-two
The couple's eldest son; dies of throat cancer at twenty-two
Lucas's parents; John faces bankruptcy and asks Lucas to return to the farm
Lucas's sister, whose husband's drinking drained her father's money
The psychiatrist who suggests that Isabelle should be institutionalised

p: Lucas is loyal, patient and practical. He puts his family before his own ambitions (he gives up the mechanic's job for the farm and later gives up work for Isabelle). He faces repeated loss with quiet strength. Many readers see him as a hero of ordinary life.

Place: the main setting is the small farming town of Alexandria, Ontario, about an hour from Ottawa. Other places include Uxbridge, Kemptville, Cornwall (the hospital and a paper mill) and Ottawa (the cancer unit). Time: two timelines: the present hospital vigil, and a past that begins in the late summer of 1956 and covers several decades. Atmosphere: a close rural community, warm but marked by hardship, illness and loss.

The farm and the town ground the story in ordinary working life, so the suffering of the family is easy to relate to. The hospital frame gives the story its urgency: Lucas is racing to complete his story while Lucy is in danger.

title: Path of Lucas: Themes and Narrative Technique
summary: Love, devotion, endurance and loss as themes; symbolism of the butterfly; and the frame story and flashbacks as technique.

p: Devotion and love: Lucas's long loyalty to Isabelle and his children. Endurance through loss: the death of friends and relatives, the illness and death of his son and wife, and his daughter's coma. Family duty and sacrifice: he gives up his career for the farm and later for his wife. Memory and storytelling: telling a story keeps a person and a family alive. Grief and hope: the dead are remembered with love and the living continue.
The monarch butterfly: Lucas reads it as a sign of Richard's and Isabelle's release from pain. It stands for spirit, change and comfort. The story itself acts as a lifeline for Lucy.

Frame story: the hospital vigil surrounds the life story. This gives the story a purpose and a deadline. Flashbacks: scenes from the past, in order, tell the long life of the family. The dual timeline lets the reader see how the past shapes the present. Tone: warm and simple, moving between sadness and comfort. (Check in the book who tells the story at each stage, because your lesson note's statement that the whole novel is in the first person with a wheelchair athlete as narrator is not supported by published descriptions.)

sections.h: Model answer: the theme of endurance
p: Lucas endures repeated losses: friends, a nephew, his sister-in-law, his son and finally his wife. Each time he does not give up; he stays with Isabelle in her depression, nurses Richard and keeps his family together. The novel suggests that endurance is not only strength of body but loyalty, patience and love over many years.

The 'path' of the title is Lucas's long journey through life, with its hard choices and losses, which he walks again by telling it to Lucy. The word 'path' also suggests the road on which he first meets Isabelle.

title: Comparing Redemption Road and Path of Lucas
summary: A corrected comparison table of the two novels and a plan for the comparative essay.

p: Study the table. It is based on published descriptions of the books, not on the lesson note's version. Check each entry against your copy.

head: Feature
Redemption Road (Elma Shaw)
Path of Lucas (Susanne Bellefeuille)
rows: Post-war Liberia (Africa), a country recovering from civil war
Rural Ontario, Canada, over several decades
Bendu Lewis, a young woman who counsels war victims
Lucas Clarkson, a farmer's son who becomes a loyal husband and father
Bendu against her past and against the man who wronged her; confession against silence
Lucas against loss, illness and hardship; endurance against despair
War: collective trauma, rape, child soldiers, impunity
Personal and family tragedies: death, illness, abuse, mental illness
Present and flashbacks to the war
Hospital frame story and flashbacks to a long life
Devotion, endurance, family duty, grief and hope
Bitter-sweet: Lucy wakes while Lucas dies; memory is passed on

p: Both show characters who have suffered deeply and keep going. Both use memory and flashback. Both end with a measure of hope. Both show how family support helps people to endure.

Redemption Road is about a nation's trauma and the need for justice; Path of Lucas is about a family's life across decades. Redemption Road has a human villain; in Path of Lucas the main opponents are loss, illness and time.

sections.h: Essay plan: compare the central conflict and the type of trauma
p: Introduction: both explore endurance and healing. Paragraph 1: the central conflict in each (with one event from each book). Paragraph 2: the type of trauma, collective against personal. Paragraph 3: how the setting (Africa and Canada) shapes the story. Conclusion: what the two novels together teach about human strength.

title: Second Term Revision: Prose Terms and the Two Novels
summary: A checklist for the term, exam technique for prose and a reminder to always read the set texts.

p: Prose terms: plot (Freytag's pyramid), character types, setting, theme, point of view. Redemption Road: author and context, the story, characters, setting, themes, technique. Path of Lucas: author and context, the story, characters, setting, themes and technique. Comparison of the novels.

1. Underline the key words in the question (character, theme, setting, compare). 2. Plan three points. 3. Begin each paragraph with a clear point, support it with an event or short quotation from the book, then explain it. 4. Link back to the question. 5. Keep to the time.

Your lesson note for both novels gives 'likely events' that do not match published descriptions of the books. The only way to be safe in the examination is to read the novels themselves. Read at least once, and then re-read the important chapters. Prepare a one-page summary in your own words with names, places and events from your own copy.

What is the climax of Redemption Road? Check in your book; published guides place the climax in the kidnapping and escape followed by Bendu's confession. What is the symbol of the title? A road: a journey from guilt to healing. What is a frame story? A story inside which another story is told, as in Path of Lucas, where Lucas's life story is told by a hospital bed.
